claim_checks.claim: PostgreSQL implements multi-version concurrency control (MVCC) by creating copies (versions) of tuples as they are modified and removing the old versions once the transactions that can see them have ended
claim_checks.page_says: MVCC is implemented by creating copies (versions) of tuples as they are modified
claim_checks.note: The glossary goes on to say the old versions need to be removed after the transactions that can see them terminate.

claim_checks.claim: Transaction IDs (XIDs) are 32 bits wide and compared with modulo-2^32 arithmetic, so it is necessary to vacuum every table in every database at least once every two billion transactions; in PostgreSQL 19 the server starts warning when the oldest XIDs are one hundred million transactions from the wraparound point and refuses to assign new XIDs once fewer than three million are left
claim_checks.page_says: Normal XIDs are compared using modulo-232 arithmetic.
claim_checks.note: The manual says normal XIDs use modulo-2^32 comparison; FrozenTransactionId and BootstrapTransactionId do not follow it (see 3.2 item 2). The summary drops the word 'normal'. The 32-bit width, the two-billion vacuum rule and the 100 million / 3 million margins are entailed.

claim_checks.claim: In PostgreSQL an UPDATE or DELETE of a row does not immediately remove the old version: that version must not be deleted while it is still potentially visible to other transactions, and VACUUM later removes such dead row versions and marks their space for reuse
claim_checks.page_says: does not immediately remove the old version of the row

claim_checks.claim: Visibility depends on comparing XIDs, and since XIDs have only 32 bits, a cluster that runs for more than 4 billion transactions would suffer transaction ID wraparound: transactions in the past suddenly appear to be in the future and their output becomes invisible, which the manual calls catastrophic data loss even though the data is still there
claim_checks.page_says: (more than 4 billion transactions) would suffer transaction ID wraparound

claim_checks.claim: Freezing is the cure: VACUUM marks rows as frozen once their inserting transaction committed far enough in the past that its effects are certain to be visible to all current and future transactions
claim_checks.page_says: inserted by a transaction that committed sufficiently far in the past

claim_checks.claim: `xmin` is the row's insertion XID, visible as a system column; `xmax` is a field of the tuple header, where a multixact ID is stored when several transactions lock the row
claim_checks.page_says: only the multixact ID appears in the xmax field in the tuple header

claim_checks.claim: Transaction ID (XID) and epoch: the unique, sequentially assigned number a transaction receives when it first causes a database modification, only 32 bits wide on disk; a 32-bit epoch extends it, and in some contexts epoch and XID are considered together as a single 64-bit value
claim_checks.page_says: When stored on disk, xids are only 32-bits wide

claim_checks.claim: MVCC snapshot: a `SnapshotData` structure; the same structure also represents special snapshots with non-MVCC semantics
claim_checks.page_says: "special" snapshots that have non-MVCC semantics

claim_checks.claim: Visibility map: two bits per page: all-visible (all tuples on the page are visible to all transactions) and all-frozen (all tuples on the page are marked frozen)
claim_checks.page_says: The second one (all-frozen) indicates that all tuples in the page are marked frozen.

claim_checks.claim: `pg_class.relfrozenxid` holds a table's oldest unfrozen XID left at the end of the last VACUUM that advanced it; `pg_database.datfrozenxid` is the minimum of those per-table values
claim_checks.page_says: it is just the minimum of the per-table relfrozenxid values within the database

claim_checks.claim: A multixact ID encodes lock information when more than one transaction locks a row at once; `pg_class.relminmxid` stores the oldest multixact ID that may still appear in the table
claim_checks.page_says: stores the oldest possible multixact ID still appearing in any tuple of that table

claim_checks.section: ### 3.1 Which row versions a snapshot sees
claim_checks.claim: Under an MVCC snapshot a tuple is visible if and only if it is valid for that snapshot: the effects of all transactions committed as of the snapshot and of previous commands of the own transaction count, while transactions shown as in progress by the snapshot, transactions started after it was taken and changes made by the current command do not
claim_checks.page_says: A tuple is visible iff the tuple is valid for the given MVCC snapshot.

claim_checks.section: ### 3.1 Which row versions a snapshot sees
claim_checks.claim: The snapshot can never see the effects of XIDs at or above its `xmax` and can see all older XIDs except those listed in `xip`, the XIDs in progress when it was taken (empty for a snapshot taken during recovery); its `xmin` is stored only as an optimization, so that most tuples need no search of the XID arrays
claim_checks.page_says: It can see the effects of all older XIDs except those listed in the snapshot. | (and other transactions that are in progress if taken during recovery)
claim_checks.note: The header excludes every XID listed in the snapshot, which means xip and also subxip. subxip holds in-progress subtransactions, and during recovery it holds the in-progress transactions while xip is empty. Naming only xip, with 'empty during recovery', implies that a recovery snapshot sees every older XID, which is a wider visible set than the header gives. 'Stored only as an optimization' also adds an 'only' the header lacks: it also says xmin is used specially by HeapTupleSatisfiesDirty and NonVacuumable.

claim_checks.section: ### 3.1 Which row versions a snapshot sees
claim_checks.claim: Vacuum asks a different question with a non-vacuumable snapshot: a tuple is visible if it might be visible to some transaction, and vacuumable if it is surely dead to everyone, judged against an xmin horizon
claim_checks.page_says: A tuple is visible iff the tuple might be visible to some transaction
claim_checks.note: The header defines SNAPSHOT_NON_VACUUMABLE and its xmin horizon, but nowhere says that VACUUM uses this snapshot type. The definition is entailed; the claim that VACUUM asks its question with this snapshot is not. The saved vacuumlazy.c, which this claim does not cite, shows VACUUM calling HeapTupleSatisfiesVacuum against cutoffs.OldestXmin.

claim_checks.section: ### 3.2 Why the horizon is about two billion
claim_checks.claim: Normal XIDs are compared using modulo-2^32 arithmetic, so every normal XID has two billion older and two billion newer XIDs, and a row version created with a normal XID appears to be in the past for the next two billion transactions but suddenly appears to be in the future if it still exists after more than two billion
claim_checks.page_says: If the row version still exists after more than two billion transactions, it will suddenly appear to be in the future.

claim_checks.section: ### 3.2 Why the horizon is about two billion
claim_checks.claim: `FrozenTransactionId` (2) does not follow the normal comparison rules and is always considered older than every normal XID, as is `BootstrapTransactionId` (1), which system catalogs may contain in rows inserted during the first phase of initdb; before PostgreSQL 9.4 freezing replaced the row's insertion XID with `FrozenTransactionId`, while newer versions set a flag bit and keep the original `xmin` for forensic use
claim_checks.page_says: Newer versions just set a flag bit, preserving the row's original xmin for possible forensic use.

claim_checks.section: ### 3.2 Why the horizon is about two billion
claim_checks.claim: When the counter reaches the maximum XID value it starts over at 3, because the values under that are reserved, and the epoch is incremented by one
claim_checks.page_says: it starts over at 3 (values under that are reserved) and the epoch value is incremented by one

claim_checks.section: ### 3.2 Why the horizon is about two billion
claim_checks.claim: The server's own limit arithmetic puts the point of real trouble, `xidWrapLimit`, halfway around the XID space from the oldest `datfrozenxid` (`oldest_datfrozenxid + (MaxTransactionId >> 1)`), and its comment notes that the special XIDs make the loop a little smaller
claim_checks.page_says: because the special XIDs reduce the size of the loop a little bit

claim_checks.claim: VACUUM uses the visibility map to choose pages and normally skips pages without dead row versions even if they hold old XIDs, so normal VACUUMs won't always freeze every old row version; a normal vacuum may also eagerly scan some all-visible but not all-frozen pages to freeze them, which reduces the pages the next aggressive vacuum must scan
claim_checks.page_says: Therefore, normal VACUUMs won't always freeze every old row version in the table.

claim_checks.claim: An aggressive vacuum freezes all eligible unfrozen XID and MXID values, and `relfrozenxid` advances only when every page that might contain unfrozen XIDs is scanned: when `relfrozenxid` is more than `vacuum_freeze_table_age` old, when VACUUM's FREEZE option is used, or when all pages not already all-frozen happen to need vacuuming
claim_checks.page_says: the relfrozenxid will only be advanced when every page of the table that might contain unfrozen XIDs is scanned

claim_checks.claim: A table can go unvacuumed for at most two billion transactions minus the `vacuum_freeze_min_age` of its last aggressive vacuum, so autovacuum is invoked on any table that might contain unfrozen XIDs older than `autovacuum_freeze_max_age`, even if autovacuum is disabled; unlike a normal autovacuum, this one is not automatically interrupted by a conflicting lock request, and it shows `(to prevent wraparound)` at the end of its query in `pg_stat_activity`, or `autovacuum_wraparound` in the `started_by` column of `pg_stat_progress_vacuum`
claim_checks.page_says: (This will happen even if autovacuum is disabled.) | the autovacuum is not automatically interrupted

claim_checks.claim: The autovacuum launcher gives priority to databases at risk of XID or multixact ID wraparound, and within a database PostgreSQL 19 scores tables, with an XID component that increases greatly once a table's age passes `vacuum_failsafe_age`; before PostgreSQL 19, tables were taken in the order `pg_class` lists them
claim_checks.page_says: this component increases greatly once the age surpasses vacuum_failsafe_age

claim_checks.section: ### 3.4 Escalation as the oldest XID ages
claim_checks.claim: The checks run each time a backend asks for a new XID, against limits computed from the oldest datfrozenxid: past `xidVacLimit` (`oldest_datfrozenxid + autovacuum_freeze_max_age`) the backend signals the postmaster to start the autovacuum launcher, once every 65,536 XIDs; past `xidWarnLimit` (`xidWrapLimit - 100000000`, a limit the source says it will not make configurable) it logs a WARNING; past `xidStopLimit` (`xidWrapLimit - 3000000`) it raises an ERROR, but only under the postmaster, which leaves single-user mode as an escape hatch for the database administrator (DBA)
claim_checks.page_says: we issue the autovac request only once per 64K transaction starts | refuse to execute transactions, unless we are running in single-user mode
claim_checks.note: GetNewTransactionId checks xid % 65536 and IsUnderPostmaster; the limit formulas match SetTransactionIdLimit (the FirstNormalTransactionId adjustments are omitted but do not change the formulas given).

claim_checks.section: ### 3.4 Escalation as the oldest XID ages
claim_checks.claim: When a table's `relfrozenxid` reaches `vacuum_failsafe_age`, VACUUM stops applying any cost-based delay, bypasses further non-essential maintenance such as index vacuuming, and disables any Buffer Access Strategy, so it may use all of shared buffers
claim_checks.page_says: any Buffer Access Strategy in use will be disabled resulting in VACUUM being free to make use of all of shared buffers

claim_checks.section: ### 3.4 Escalation as the oldest XID ages
claim_checks.claim: In the `REL_19_0` source the failsafe also bypasses heap vacuuming and heap truncation, is checked each time VACUUM scans another 4GB of pages, and logs a WARNING that it is bypassing nonessential maintenance of the table because its `relfrozenxid` or `relminmxid` is too far in the past
claim_checks.page_says: Perform a failsafe check each time we scan another 4GB of pages.

claim_checks.section: ### 3.4 Escalation as the oldest XID ages
claim_checks.claim: Once fewer than three million XIDs are left, transactions already in progress can continue, only read-only transactions can be started, operations that modify database records or truncate relations fail, and the VACUUM command can still be run normally
claim_checks.page_says: Operations that modify database records or truncate relations will fail.

claim_checks.section: ### 3.5 What holds the oldest XID back
claim_checks.claim: The manual's recovery steps name the holders and where to find them: old prepared transactions in `pg_prepared_xacts` (large `age(transactionid)`), long-running open transactions in `pg_stat_activity` (large `age(backend_xid)` or `age(backend_xmin)`), and old replication slots in `pg_replication_slots` (large `age(xmin)` or `age(catalog_xmin)`)
claim_checks.page_says: checking pg_prepared_xacts for rows where age(transactionid) is large

claim_checks.section: ### 3.5 What holds the oldest XID back
claim_checks.claim: pganalyze adds that with `hot_standby_feedback` on, queries on a standby hold back the xmin horizon as if they ran on the primary and a lagging or stale replica's physical slot can leave it stuck, that a logical-replication subscriber stopped by a schema mismatch holds back the publisher's system-catalog xmin until replication resumes, and that a long transaction in one database does not stop the cleanup of tables in another
claim_checks.page_says: will hold back the xmin horizon just as if they were running on the primary
claim_checks.note: Claim about PostgreSQL behaviour, outside pganalyze's rank_scope: rated Rank 4 by class, which role 3 allows.

claim_checks.claim: The members of a multixact are stored separately in `pg_multixact`, with only the multixact ID in the tuple's `xmax`; multixact IDs are a 32-bit counter like XIDs, and MXIDs have the same margins, a warning one hundred million from the wraparound point and a refusal below three million, but MXID exhaustion blocks only writes whose row locks need an MXID, while XID exhaustion blocks all writes
claim_checks.page_says: XID exhaustion will block all write transactions, but MXID exhaustion will only block a subset of write transactions

claim_checks.claim: Inserting a child row takes `SELECT … FOR KEY SHARE` on the referenced parent row, so concurrent inserts lock parent rows and those locks become MultiXacts; savepoints do the same when different sub-transactions lock or modify the same row, and every PL/pgSQL EXCEPTION clause creates a savepoint
claim_checks.page_says: PostgreSQL uses a SELECT…FOR KEY SHARE on the table referenced by the foreign key

claim_checks.claim: MultiXacts are immutable, so each new share-locker of a row creates a new MultiXact holding all earlier members: quoting PostgreSQL developer Thomas Munro, n lockers make n - 1 multixacts and (n * (n + 1)) / 2 - 1 members, for example 4 MultiXacts with 14 members for 5 transactions
claim_checks.page_says: so that's n - 1 multixacts and (n * (n + 1)) / 2 - 1 members
claim_checks.note: Rank 4 source in role 3: allowed. The 5-transaction example is Metronome's own, next to the quote.

claim_checks.claim: Whenever VACUUM scans part of a table it replaces multixact IDs older than `vacuum_multixact_freeze_min_age`; a `relminmxid` older than `vacuum_multixact_freeze_table_age` forces an aggressive vacuum, a multixact age above `autovacuum_multixact_freeze_max_age` forces one even if autovacuum is nominally disabled, and once member entries exceed approximately 2 billion (roughly 10GB in `pg_multixact/members`) aggressive scans occur more often for all tables, oldest first
claim_checks.page_says: aggressive vacuum scans will occur more often for all tables, starting with those that have the oldest multixact-age

claim_checks.claim: On one run (gcc in the harness's `linlab:1` image, kernel 7.2.12-orbstack), the `varsup.c` formulas with `MaxTransactionId` taken as 4,294,967,295 printed `warn_age=2047483647 stop_age=2144483647`, a hard stop at an XID age of about 2.14 billion, and, for 99,985,967 XIDs left, `pct=4.66%`, the figure in the DETAIL line of the manual's sample warning
claim_checks.page_says: probe-01 stdout: warn_age=2047483647 stop_age=2144483647 wrap_age=2147483647 / left=99985967 pct=4.66% | manual: DETAIL: Approximately 4.66% of transaction ID space remains before wraparound.
claim_checks.note: Probe status pass. Its code computes the varsup.c limit formulas and the errdetail percentage formula ((double) left / (MaxTransactionId / 2) * 100) and prints the results; it cannot print the expected line whatever happens. The MaxTransactionId value is an assumption the claim states. Worded as one run with its image. The manual part is entailed.

claim_checks.claim: On one run (gcc in the harness's `linlab:1` image, kernel 7.2.12-orbstack), comparing by the sign of the 32-bit difference printed that a row stamped XID 100 is still in the past 2.0 billion XIDs later but in the future 2.2 billion later, and that XID 4294967000 counts as older than XID 100; this C function illustrates the circle the manual describes and is not PostgreSQL's own comparison code
claim_checks.page_says: probe-02 stdout: after 2.0e9: past / after 2.2e9: future / 4294967000 vs 100: older
claim_checks.note: Probe status pass. The code computes each result from the signed 32-bit difference and prints it; the claim says plainly that the function is the doc's own, not PostgreSQL's.

claim_checks.claim: The manual's two queries report the age of each table, taking the older of the table and its TOAST table (linked through `reltoastrelid`), and of each database; the age is the number of transactions from the cutoff XID to the current transaction's XID
claim_checks.page_says: The age column measures the number of transactions from the cutoff XID to the current transaction's XID.

claim_checks.claim: In Crunchy Data's worked example, the per-database query returned `postgres` at 170,604,895 and `mydb` at 169,088,197 against an `autovacuum_freeze_max_age` of 200000000, and the per-table query over tables, TOAST tables and materialized views listed `pg_proc` first at 170,606,208 (936 kB)
claim_checks.page_says: WHERE relkind IN ('r', 't', 'm') AND n.nspname NOT IN ('pg_toast')
claim_checks.note: The output values are entailed. The per-table query also filters out the pg_toast schema, a condition the claim drops while describing the query as covering TOAST tables.

claim_checks.claim: The PostgreSQL 19 manual shows `pg_get_multixact_stats()` reporting multixact usage, with a sample of 311,740,299 multixact IDs and 2,785,241,176 member entries in 13 GB

pganalyze finds the holders of §3.5 with `pg_stat_activity` ordered by `greatest(age(backend_xmin), age(backend_xid))`, `pg_stat_replication` ordered by `age(backend_xmin)` for standbys and `pg_prepared_xacts` ordered by `age(transaction)`, and ends them with `pg_cancel_backend` (active query) or `pg_terminate_backend` (idle in transaction), both of which roll the transaction back, or with `COMMIT PREPARED` / `ROLLBACK PREPARED`
claim_checks.page_says: ORDER BY greatest(age(backend_xmin), age(backend_xid)) DESC; | Note this will roll back the transaction
claim_checks.note: The page's roll-back note follows the sentence that offers the two cancel commands as alternatives.

claim_checks.claim: The AWS (Amazon Web Services) RDS user guide's sample strategy sets `autovacuum_freeze_max_age` to 200 million, raises a low-severity alarm when a table reaches 500 million unfrozen transactions, treats 1 billion as an alarm to take action on, and raises a high-severity alarm at 1.5 billion that it recommends resolving immediately
claim_checks.page_says: If a table reaches 1.5 billion unvacuumed transactions, that triggers a high-severity alarm.

claim_checks.claim: Crunchy Data alerts on `percent_towards_wraparound` (age against 2 billion), whose 100% should be acted upon immediately, and on `percent_towards_emergency_autovac`, which watches for a table reaching `autovacuum_freeze_max_age`
claim_checks.page_says: this alert hitting 100% should be acted upon immediately
claim_checks.note: The page says the metric watches the database's highest TXID age, which datfrozenxid takes from its oldest table.

claim_checks.claim: pganalyze checks every 30 minutes and by default raises a warning when the server's xmin horizon was assigned more than 24 hours ago, even if no VACUUM is blocked yet
claim_checks.page_says: Detects when the xmin horizon on the server was assigned more than 24 hours ago
claim_checks.note: Claim about pganalyze's own check: inside its rank_scope (Rank 1).

claim_checks.claim: Sentry's hosted service was down for most of the US working day on Monday, July 20 (2015), running read-only with replicas serving reads; the team let the running autovacuums finish rather than restart, one of them failed or did nothing with no trace in the non-verbose logs, and with every relation but one huge event-mapping table vacuumed, truncating that table restored the system five minutes later
claim_checks.page_says: Five minutes later, the system was fully restored.

claim_checks.claim: Sentry named as causes too high an `autovacuum_freeze_max_age`, the default of 3 autovacuum workers and far too much vacuum delay, and moved to `autovacuum_freeze_max_age = 500000000`, `autovacuum_max_workers = 6`, `autovacuum_naptime = '15s'`, `autovacuum_vacuum_cost_delay = 0`, `maintenance_work_mem = '10GB'` and `vacuum_freeze_min_age = 10000000`
claim_checks.page_says: the default of 3 autovacuum workers | autovacuum_freeze_max_age = 500000000

claim_checks.section: ### 4.7 Incident: Metronome, May 2025 (MultiXact members, Aurora PostgreSQL 13.18)
claim_checks.claim: Metronome had four outages between May 10 and May 17, 2025, each lasting over an hour, that severely impacted write operations on an AWS Aurora PostgreSQL 13.18 cluster exceeding 30TB: crossing a global limit on MultiXact members triggered emergency vacuums and PostgreSQL's defensive lockout of write operations until they completed, a recovery that takes several hours for their larger tables
claim_checks.page_says: This led to PostgreSQL's defensive lockout of write operations until these vacuums could complete

claim_checks.claim: `vacuum_freeze_min_age` is the cutoff age for freezing pages with an older XID (default 50 million, settable from zero to one billion, silently limited to half of `autovacuum_freeze_max_age`); `vacuum_freeze_table_age` is the `relfrozenxid` age at which VACUUM scans aggressively (default 150 million, zero to two billion, silently limited to 95% of `autovacuum_freeze_max_age`); `autovacuum_freeze_max_age` forces a VACUUM to prevent wraparound even when autovacuum is otherwise disabled (default 200 million, can only be set at server start, can be reduced per table through storage parameters); `vacuum_failsafe_age` defaults to 1.6 billion, accepts zero to 2.1 billion and is silently adjusted to no less than 105% of `autovacuum_freeze_max_age`
claim_checks.page_says: VACUUM will silently limit the effective value to half the value of autovacuum_freeze_max_age

claim_checks.claim: `autovacuum_multixact_freeze_max_age` defaults to 400 million multixacts and can only be set at server start; `vacuum_multixact_freeze_table_age` defaults to 150 million (zero to two billion, limited to 95% of `autovacuum_multixact_freeze_max_age`); `vacuum_multixact_freeze_min_age` defaults to 5 million (zero to one billion, limited to half of it); `vacuum_multixact_failsafe_age` defaults to 1.6 billion (zero to 2.1 billion, no less than 105% of it), and when that failsafe triggers, cost-based delay stops and non-essential tasks are bypassed
claim_checks.page_says: which is why the default is a relatively low 400 million multixacts

claim_checks.claim: `vacuum_max_eager_freeze_failure_rate` is the fraction of pages VACUUM may scan and fail to set all-frozen before it disables eager scanning: 0 disables eager scanning, the default is 0.03 (3%), and successful eager freezes are capped internally at 20% of the all-visible but not all-frozen pages
claim_checks.page_says: Successful page freezes are capped internally at 20% of the all-visible but not all-frozen pages

claim_checks.claim: The `REL_19_0` source builds these messages (the values above are the manual's sample), raises the error with code `ERRCODE_PROGRAM_LIMIT_EXCEEDED`, and gives each hint a second line about prepared transactions and replication slots, which the manual's printed samples leave out
claim_checks.page_says: errcode(ERRCODE_PROGRAM_LIMIT_EXCEEDED) | You might also need to commit or roll back old prepared transactions, or drop stale replication slots.
claim_checks.note: The message block in 5.2 matches the source's errmsg, errdetail and errhint strings; the manual's samples print one-line hints.

claim_checks.claim: Resolve old prepared transactions, which should be committed or rolled back; end long-running open transactions, which should be committed or rolled back, or whose session can be terminated with `pg_terminate_backend`; drop old replication slots, knowing that if a slot's server still exists and might still connect to it, that replica may need to be rebuilt
claim_checks.page_says: that replica may need to be rebuilt

claim_checks.claim: Execute VACUUM in the target database, database-wide (simplest) or on the tables with the oldest XIDs, and the VACUUM should be performed by a superuser, else it fails to process system catalogs and cannot advance `datfrozenxid`; do not use VACUUM FULL, which requires an XID and will therefore fail, except in what the manual calls super-user mode, where it consumes an XID and increases the risk of wraparound; do not use VACUUM FREEZE either, because it does more than the minimum work; once normal operation is restored, ensure that autovacuum is properly configured in the target database
claim_checks.page_says: Do not use VACUUM FULL in this scenario, because it requires an XID and will therefore fail, except in super-user mode

claim_checks.claim: Stopping the postmaster or entering single-user mode is not necessary or desirable to restore normal operation: in typical scenarios it should be avoided whenever possible, since it takes the system down and disables the wraparound safeguards, and its only use here is to TRUNCATE or DROP unneeded tables, which the three-million-transaction margin exists for
claim_checks.page_says: The three-million-transaction safety margin exists to let the administrator do this.

claim_checks.claim: MXID exhaustion: the same steps apply, except that running and prepared transactions can be ignored when they cannot appear in a multixact, and replication slots do not directly hold back multixact cleanup
claim_checks.page_says: Unlike transaction ID wraparound, replication slots do not directly hold back multixact cleanup.

claim_checks.claim: Autovacuum thresholds and many other autovacuum parameters can be overridden per table through storage parameters, and for insert-mostly tables it may be beneficial to lower the table's `autovacuum_freeze_min_age`; temporary tables cannot be accessed by autovacuum, so they should be vacuumed and analyzed through session SQL commands
claim_checks.page_says: Temporary tables cannot be accessed by autovacuum.

claim_checks.claim: Raising `autovacuum_freeze_max_age`: its sole disadvantage is more space in `pg_xact` and `pg_commit_ts` (about half a gigabyte and 20GB at the maximum of two billion, against about 50MB and 2GB at the default), and the manual recommends the maximum when that is trivial against the database size; one disadvantage of lowering `vacuum_freeze_min_age` is that VACUUM might do useless work, freezing rows that are modified soon after
claim_checks.page_says: The sole disadvantage of increasing autovacuum_freeze_max_age (and vacuum_freeze_table_age along with it)

claim_checks.claim: AWS's sample keeps 200 million (§4.5) and Sentry moved to 500 million (§4.6), while for databases with a high transaction rate Crunchy Data's author has often set 1 billion, but only when sure wraparound is monitored and the disk space is available
claim_checks.page_says: I've often set this value to 1 billion without much issue

claim_checks.claim: Crunchy Data's author calls it perfectly safe to cancel the emergency vacuum when it causes lock contention, but it keeps restarting until that vacuum completes or a manual vacuum is run
claim_checks.page_says: it's perfectly safe to cancel it to allow your other transactions to finish

claim_checks.claim: A lock request that conflicts with a normal autovacuum's SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE lock interrupts it, and regularly running such commands, ANALYZE for example, can effectively prevent autovacuums from ever completing
claim_checks.page_says: can effectively prevent autovacuums from ever completing

claim_checks.page_says: maintenance_work_mem has a hard internal limit of 1GB for the relevant paths

claim_checks.claim: Metronome, on Aurora PostgreSQL 13.18, describes a hard limit of approximately 4 billion members across all MultiXacts and says PostgreSQL exposes no metric for member space consumption
claim_checks.page_says: This space has a hard limit of approximately 4 billion total members across all MultiXacts.

claim_checks.page_says: which cannot wrap around but must also be managed to keep disk usage under control

claim_checks.claim: Percona's 2022 post says the service is forced to shut down and quotes a hint reading "To avoid a database shutdown", and Crunchy Data's 2019 post says the database will be forced to shut down
claim_checks.page_says: the PostgreSQL service is forced to shut down | the database will be forced to shut down

claim_checks.claim: That is wrong for PostgreSQL 19: the server refuses to assign new XIDs, while read-only transactions can still start and VACUUM can still be run (§3.4), and the `REL_19_0` hint reads "To avoid transaction ID assignment failures"
claim_checks.page_says: only read-only transactions can be started | To avoid transaction ID assignment failures

claim_checks.claim: Percona gives a countdown from 10 million and read-only mode at 1 million, and Sentry says commands stop with fewer than one million left
claim_checks.page_says: 1 million transactions before the upper limit is reached, PostgreSQL goes into read-only mode. | stop accepting commands when there are fewer than one million transactions left

claim_checks.claim: In PostgreSQL 19 the warning starts 100,000,000 and the stop 3,000,000 transactions before `xidWrapLimit`
claim_checks.page_says: xidStopLimit = xidWrapLimit - 3000000; | xidWarnLimit = xidWrapLimit - 100000000;

claim_checks.claim: Percona's recovery procedure is a cluster-wide VACUUM in single-user mode (`postgres --single`), and Sentry cites restarting in single-user mode as general advice
claim_checks.page_says: performing a cluster-wide vacuum in single-user mode | One piece of general advice is to stop the database and restart in single-user mode

claim_checks.claim: The PostgreSQL 19 manual says this was sometimes recommended in earlier releases and is not necessary or desirable now, since in the stopped state the VACUUM command can still be run normally
claim_checks.page_says: contrary to what was sometimes recommended in earlier releases, it is not necessary or desirable

claim_checks.claim: Sentry calls such advice awful, and Percona lists autovacuum turned off among the causes of wraparound
claim_checks.page_says: The internet is full of awful advice from users suggesting you should turn off autovacuum | Autovacuum is turned off.

claim_checks.claim: Turning autovacuum off does not stop the anti-wraparound runs, because the system launches autovacuum processes to prevent wraparound even when autovacuum is otherwise disabled
claim_checks.page_says: the system will launch autovacuum processes to prevent wraparound even when autovacuum is otherwise disabled

claim_checks.claim: Metronome's metrics showed MultiXact ID use below 50% of the threshold, and emergency vacuums began at around 200 million MultiXact IDs although `autovacuum_multixact_freeze_max_age` was 400 million, because the separate member space limit was hit first
claim_checks.page_says: (less than 50% utilization) | causing emergency vacuums at around 200m MultiXact IDs

claim_checks.claim: Member entries are a second budget, separate from MXID age: once multixact member entries exceed approximately 2 billion, PostgreSQL 19 runs aggressive vacuum scans more often for all tables (§3.6), and `pg_get_multixact_stats()` reports the member count and size (§4.4)
claim_checks.page_says: if the number of multixact member entries created exceeds approximately 2 billion entries

claim_checks.claim: In the AWS Database Blog demo a standard VACUUM left the MultiXact in the row's `xmax`, because it only releases MultiXact IDs older than `vacuum_multixact_freeze_min_age`, and only VACUUM FREEZE cleared it
claim_checks.page_says: the XMAX field will be cleared only after a VACUUM FREEZE cleanup is performed

claim_checks.claim: Read-only transactions do too: vacuum must retain the information they may need until they close, for both XIDs and MultiXacts
claim_checks.page_says: For read-only transactions: Vacuum must retain its information until the transaction is closed.

claim_checks.claim: The standard VACUUM does not return space to the operating system, except when pages at the end of a table become entirely free and an exclusive table lock can be easily obtained, while VACUUM FULL rewrites the whole table, can take a long time and needs extra disk space for the new copy; in the stopped state it fails because it requires an XID (§5.3, rule 2)
claim_checks.page_says: it requires an XID and will therefore fail, except in super-user mode
claim_checks.note: The space-return and rewrite parts are entailed. The manual makes the VACUUM FULL failure conditional: in super-user mode it instead consumes an XID. The sentence drops that exception, although the rule it points to keeps it.

claim_checks.claim: The wraparound paragraph of the manual says the XID counter "wraps around to zero"
claim_checks.page_says: the XID counter wraps around to zero

claim_checks.claim: The manual motivates XID comparison with a row whose insertion XID is greater than the current transaction's XID being "in the future"
claim_checks.page_says: a row version with an insertion XID greater than the current transaction's XID is “in the future”

claim_checks.claim: The AWS RDS user guide says that when a database's age reaches 2 billion transaction IDs, wraparound occurs and the database becomes read-only
claim_checks.page_says: When the age of a database reaches 2 billion transaction IDs, transaction ID (XID) wraparound occurs

claim_checks.page_says: Aggressive VACUUMs are invoked when the storage occupied by MultiXacts exceeds 10 GB.

violations.section: ### 3.1 Which row versions a snapshot sees
violations.evidence: C14: item 3 says VACUUM asks its question with a non-vacuumable snapshot; snapshot.h defines SNAPSHOT_NON_VACUUMABLE but never says VACUUM uses it (unsupported).
C2: the TL;DR says XIDs are compared modulo 2^32; the manual says normal XIDs, and the special XIDs are exempt (dropped qualifier).

violations.section: ### 3.1 Which row versions a snapshot sees
violations.evidence: C13: item 2 narrows 'listed in the snapshot' to xip, which implies a recovery snapshot sees every older XID although subxip then holds the in-progress XIDs; it also adds 'only' to the xmin optimization.
C36: Crunchy's per-table query is described as covering TOAST tables, but the query excludes the pg_toast schema (dropped condition).
C74: misconception 8 says VACUUM FULL fails in the stopped state without the manual's super-user-mode exception.
C80: the reader's 'appear to be maintained separately' is stated as fact ('is kept separately').

Item 5 labels the reader comment on Percona's post as Rank 4; an unvetted reader comment is Rank 6 by class. It sits in role 6 as an open conflict, so quarantine holds, but the side's rank is misstated.
Role 6 gives concrete trade-offs as prose bullets, with no decision table for when to raise or lower the freezing settings.
